opening.text: Think about your family dinner table. It is more than a place to eat. It is where people sit down together. They talk. They laugh. They remember each other. Even on a hard day, the table pulls everyone back.
Every Sunday, the Lord sets a table for us. A small piece of bread. A small cup of water. It looks simple. But it is one of the most sacred moments of the week.
Today I want to talk about the sacrament. What it is, why the Savior gave it, and what it can do for us.

mainMessage.text: The sacrament is how we remember Jesus Christ. Each week we eat the bread and drink the water in memory of His body and blood. We renew our covenants. We are cleansed and forgiven. We are promised that His Spirit will be with us. It is a gift to be received, not only a ritual to sit through. If we come ready, it changes the week ahead.

blocks.text: We do this to remember Him.

The night before He died, Jesus ate with His apostles. He broke bread. He passed the cup. He asked them to do this again and again, so they would not forget. After His Resurrection, He gave the same invitation to the Nephites.

And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me. Likewise also the cup after supper, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you.

And this shall ye do in remembrance of my body, which I have shown unto you. And it shall be a testimony unto the Father that ye do always remember me. And if ye do always remember me ye shall have my Spirit to be with you.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles wrote this in his article “To Always Remember Him” in the April 2011 Ensign.

We should first put in place the things that make it possible to always remember Him—frequent prayer and scripture study, thoughtful study of apostolic teachings, weekly preparation to partake of the sacrament worthily, Sunday worship, and recording and remembering what the Spirit and experience teach us about discipleship.
Remembering is something we do on purpose. The sacrament is one of the ways He gave us to do it.
We renew our covenants.

When we were baptized, we made promises. The sacrament is where we say yes to those promises again. The prayers say what we are promising. We are willing to take His name upon us. We will always remember Him. We will keep His commandments.

O God, the Eternal Father, we ask thee in the name of thy Son, Jesus Christ, to bless and sanctify this bread to the souls of all those who partake of it; that they may eat in remembrance of the body of thy Son, and witness unto thee, O God, the Eternal Father, that they are willing to take upon them the name of thy Son, and always remember him, and keep his commandments which he hath given them, that they may always have his Spirit to be with them. Amen.

O God, the Eternal Father, we ask thee, in the name of thy Son, Jesus Christ, to bless and sanctify this wine to the souls of all those who drink of it, that they may do it in remembrance of the blood of thy Son, which was shed for them; that they may witness unto thee, O God, the Eternal Father, that they do always remember him, that they may have his Spirit to be with them. Amen.

And it came to pass that he said unto them: Behold, here are the waters of Mormon (for thus were they called) and now, as ye are desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people, and are willing to bear one another’s burdens, that they may be light; Yea, and are willing to mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort, and to stand as witnesses of God at all times and in all things, and in all places that ye may be in, even until death, that ye may be redeemed of God, and be numbered with those of the first resurrection, that ye may have eternal life— Now I say unto you, if this be the desire of your hearts, what have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord, as a witness before him that ye have entered into a covenant with him, that ye will serve him and keep his commandments, that he may pour out his Spirit more abundantly upon you?
President Ezra Taft Benson said this in his talk “Born of God” from the October 1985 general conference.
Almost every week they partake of the sacrament and witness anew to their Eternal Father that they are willing to take upon them the name of His Son, always remember Him, and keep His commandments.
Notice the word “anew.” Each week we start over, with the same promise and the same Savior.
We are cleansed.

The sacrament is not only about what we promise. It is also about what the Lord gives. When we come with a broken heart and a contrite spirit, He renews the cleansing we first received at baptism. The Savior’s blood was shed “for the remission of sins.”

And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body. And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it; For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.

Thou shalt offer a sacrifice unto the Lord thy God in righteousness, even that of a broken heart and a contrite spirit. And that thou mayest more fully keep thyself unspotted from the world, thou shalt go to the house of prayer and offer up thy sacraments upon my holy day;
President Dallin H. Oaks, First Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “The Aaronic Priesthood and the Sacrament” from the October 2019 general conference.

We are commanded to repent of our sins and to come to the Lord with a broken heart and a contrite spirit and partake of the sacrament in compliance with its covenants. When we renew our baptismal covenants in this way, the Lord renews the cleansing effect of our baptism.
We do not have to carry last week’s mistakes into next week. That is what the sacrament offers.
We are promised His Spirit.
The prayers end with a promise: “that they may always have his Spirit to be with them.” When the Savior gave the sacrament to the Nephites, they were filled. They felt it. They cried out in praise.

And he said unto them: He that eateth this bread eateth of my body to his soul; and he that drinketh of this wine drinketh of my blood to his soul; and his soul shall never hunger nor thirst, but shall be filled. Now, when the multitude had all eaten and drunk, behold, they were filled with the Spirit; and they did cry out with one voice, and gave glory to Jesus, whom they both saw and heard.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Always Have His Spirit” from the October 1996 general conference.

Let us qualify ourselves for our Savior’s promise that by partaking of the sacrament we will ‘be filled’ (3 Ne. 20:8; see also 3 Ne. 18:9), which means that we will be ‘filled with the Spirit’ (3 Ne. 20:9). That Spirit—the Holy Ghost—is our comforter, our direction finder, our communicator, our interpreter, our witness, and our purifier—our infallible guide and sanctifier for our mortal journey toward eternal life.
A comforter. A direction finder. An infallible guide. That is what is on offer every Sunday.
We prepare ourselves.

Paul told the Corinthians to take the sacrament with care. He did not mean that we must be perfect. He meant that we should think about what we are doing. Look at your life. Notice what needs mending. Then come.

Wherefore whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup. For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body.

Elder Jay E. Jensen of the Seventy shared this in his talk “Arms of Safety” from the October 2008 general conference. He was telling of a young man he helped, as his bishop, to repent. After a time, the young man was able to take the sacrament again.

As I sat on the stand in that sacrament meeting, my eyes were drawn to him as he now partook of the sacrament worthily. I witnessed arms of mercy, love, and safety encircling him as the healing of the Atonement warmed his soul and lifted his load, resulting in the promised forgiveness, peace, and happiness.
Preparing is not about fear. It is about making room for mercy.
We need Him every week.
We get hungry again and again. The body needs food every day. The spirit needs food, too. Jesus called Himself the bread of life. The sacrament is a weekly meal for the soul.
And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
Elder Robert D. Hales of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Out of Darkness into His Marvelous Light” from the April 2002 general conference.

When the spiritual light of the Holy Ghost is present, the darkness of Satan departs. . . . If we let the light of the Spirit flicker or fade by failing to keep the commandments or by not partaking of the sacrament or praying or studying the scriptures, the darkness of the adversary will surely come in.
The light of the Spirit does not stay on by itself. We keep it burning by coming back to the table.

story.title: Jesus gives the sacrament to the Nephites

blocks.text: After His Resurrection, Jesus visited the Nephites at the temple in Bountiful. He taught them. Then He asked for bread and wine. He wanted them to know this ordinance for themselves.

And it came to pass that Jesus commanded his disciples that they should bring forth some bread and wine unto him. And while they were gone for bread and wine, he commanded the multitude that they should sit themselves down upon the earth. And when the disciples had come with bread and wine, he took of the bread and brake and blessed it; and he gave unto the disciples and commanded that they should eat. And when they had eaten and were filled, he commanded that they should give unto the multitude. And when the multitude had eaten and were filled, he said unto the disciples: Behold there shall one be ordained among you, and to him will I give power that he shall break bread and bless it and give it unto the people of my church, unto all those who shall believe and be baptized in my name.
Look at how He did it. He took the bread, He broke it, and He blessed it. He gave it to His disciples first, and they gave it to everyone else. It is the same pattern we follow today.

application.text: First, this Sunday, arrive a few minutes early. Sit quietly. Think about the week that just passed. Ask yourself what you would like to leave behind. Second, listen to the sacrament prayers, word for word. Notice what you are promising and what is promised to you. Third, choose one thing to do this week to keep your promise to remember Him. It could be a prayer at night or a verse in the morning.

opening.text: Most of us know what it is like when a phone battery runs low. It dims. It slows. Then it quits at the worst time. So we plug it in. Not once a year. Every day, and sometimes more.
Our spirits work something like that. Life drains them. Stress, worry, small mistakes, and the noise of the world all wear us down. We need to be reconnected, again and again.
The sacrament is how the Lord helps us do that. I would like to talk about it today.

mainMessage.text: Every week we take bread and water in remembrance of the Savior’s body and blood. As we do, we make promises to Him, and He makes promises to us. He forgives. He strengthens. He sends His Spirit. The sacrament was given by the Savior Himself, and we should treat it as the most important part of our week. It is where we come back to Him.

blocks.text: It is how we remember.

The word the Savior used again and again was “remembrance.” He knew how easily we forget. So He gave us a simple way to bring Him to mind. He gave it to His apostles in Jerusalem, and later to the people in the Americas.

And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me. Likewise also the cup after supper, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you.

We should first put in place the things that make it possible to always remember Him—frequent prayer and scripture study, thoughtful study of apostolic teachings, weekly preparation to partake of the sacrament worthily, Sunday worship, and recording and remembering what the Spirit and experience teach us about discipleship.
The sacrament is the center of those habits. The rest of the list helps us get ready for it.
It is how we keep our promises.

The sacrament prayers are not long, but every phrase counts. We say we are willing to take His name. We say we will always remember Him. We say we will keep His commandments. That is the covenant we made when we were baptized, and we renew it.

O God, the Eternal Father, we ask thee in the name of thy Son, Jesus Christ, to bless and sanctify this bread to the souls of all those who partake of it; that they may eat in remembrance of the body of thy Son, and witness unto thee, O God, the Eternal Father, that they are willing to take upon them the name of thy Son, and always remember him, and keep his commandments which he hath given them, that they may always have his Spirit to be with them. Amen.

O God, the Eternal Father, we ask thee, in the name of thy Son, Jesus Christ, to bless and sanctify this wine to the souls of all those who drink of it, that they may do it in remembrance of the blood of thy Son, which was shed for them; that they may witness unto thee, O God, the Eternal Father, that they do always remember him, that they may have his Spirit to be with them. Amen.

And it came to pass that he said unto them: Behold, here are the waters of Mormon (for thus were they called) and now, as ye are desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people, and are willing to bear one another’s burdens, that they may be light; Yea, and are willing to mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort, and to stand as witnesses of God at all times and in all things, and in all places that ye may be in, even until death, that ye may be redeemed of God, and be numbered with those of the first resurrection, that ye may have eternal life— Now I say unto you, if this be the desire of your hearts, what have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord, as a witness before him that ye have entered into a covenant with him, that ye will serve him and keep his commandments, that he may pour out his Spirit more abundantly upon you?
President Ezra Taft Benson taught this in his talk “Born of God” from the October 1985 general conference.
Almost every week they partake of the sacrament and witness anew to their Eternal Father that they are willing to take upon them the name of His Son, always remember Him, and keep His commandments.
He said “almost every week.” Not once. Not occasionally. It is a steady habit of the faithful.
It is how we are made clean.

We are all imperfect. We all leave the chapel on Sunday and then make mistakes on Monday. The Lord knows. That is why He gave a way to be renewed. The sacrament is a weekly reminder that His blood was shed for the forgiveness of sins.

And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body. And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it; For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.

We are commanded to repent of our sins and to come to the Lord with a broken heart and a contrite spirit and partake of the sacrament in compliance with its covenants. When we renew our baptismal covenants in this way, the Lord renews the cleansing effect of our baptism.
The cleansing is real. It is renewed each time we come with a humble heart.
It is how we receive the Spirit.

The Spirit is the real power source. In the prayers and in the Savior’s own words, the promise is the same. If we always remember Him, we will have His Spirit with us. The Nephites felt this. They were filled.

And he said unto them: He that eateth this bread eateth of my body to his soul; and he that drinketh of this wine drinketh of my blood to his soul; and his soul shall never hunger nor thirst, but shall be filled. Now, when the multitude had all eaten and drunk, behold, they were filled with the Spirit; and they did cry out with one voice, and gave glory to Jesus, whom they both saw and heard.

That Spirit—the Holy Ghost—is our comforter, our direction finder, our communicator, our interpreter, our witness, and our purifier—our infallible guide and sanctifier for our mortal journey toward eternal life.
Every week the charge is renewed.
It asks us to look inward first.

Before we eat and drink, Paul says, we should examine ourselves. That is not a call to feel worse. It is a call to be honest. When we see something that needs fixing, we can bring it to the Lord. If it is serious, we can talk to our bishop.

Wherefore whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup. For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body.

As I sat on the stand in that sacrament meeting, my eyes were drawn to him as he now partook of the sacrament worthily. I witnessed arms of mercy, love, and safety encircling him as the healing of the Atonement warmed his soul and lifted his load, resulting in the promised forgiveness, peace, and happiness.
That is the goal of all of it. Not shame. Mercy, love, safety, and peace.
It keeps the light on.
Bread feeds the body for a few hours. The Savior feeds the soul in a way that lasts. He said He is the bread of life. When we eat of Him, we do not go hungry.
And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
Elder Robert D. Hales of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gave this warning, and this invitation, in his talk “Out of Darkness into His Marvelous Light” from the April 2002 general conference.

When the spiritual light of the Holy Ghost is present, the darkness of Satan departs. . . . If we let the light of the Spirit flicker or fade by failing to keep the commandments or by not partaking of the sacrament or praying or studying the scriptures, the darkness of the adversary will surely come in.
A charged battery, a lit lamp. The sacrament is how we keep both.

story.title: Manna in the wilderness

blocks.text: The Israelites were in the wilderness. They had no bread. Every morning, the Lord sent something new to eat. They had to gather it each day. They could not store it for later, and it did not last. They had to come back and gather again.

And when the dew that lay was gone up, behold, upon the face of the wilderness there lay a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground. And when the children of Israel saw it, they said one to another, It is manna: for they wist not what it was. And Moses said unto them, This is the bread which the Lord hath given you to eat.
And the house of Israel called the name thereof Manna: and it was like coriander seed, white; and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey.
Manna was a picture of the true Bread, Jesus Christ. Like the manna, the sacrament is given fresh every week. We cannot save it up. We come back and receive it again.

application.text: First, plan ahead for Sunday. Get enough sleep on Saturday. Come with a clear mind. Second, put your phone away during the sacrament. Make this the one quiet moment in your week. Third, pick one thing the Spirit tells you during the sacrament, and write it down before you leave the chapel.

opening.text: A window gets dusty slowly. You do not notice it day by day. Then one morning the sun hits it just right, and you see every smudge. So you take a cloth, wipe it down, and the light comes through again.
Our lives are like that window. Small things build up. A sharp word. A selfish choice. A prayer we skipped. None of it feels big in the moment. But over time, the light gets dim.
The sacrament is the Lord’s way of cleaning the glass. I would like to talk about it today.

mainMessage.text: The Savior gave us the sacrament so we could remember Him and start fresh. Each week, we renew our promises to Him and receive His forgiveness. He promises His Spirit in return. We are asked to come humbly and prepared. The sacrament is not a break in the meeting. It is the heart of it, and it is a gift.

blocks.text: It begins with remembering.
The Savior did not ask us to do many things on the night He was betrayed. He asked us to remember. A piece of bread. A cup. Again and again, in memory of Him. The Nephites received the same request.

It is a covenant, not just a custom.

To witness anew means to say it again, and mean it again.
It wipes the glass clean.

This is where the picture of the window helps most. The Lord does not only ask for our promises. He gives us forgiveness. The blood of Christ was shed to take away sins, and the sacrament brings that to our mind every week.

The light comes through.

Once the glass is clean, the light can come through. That is the Spirit. The prayers promise it. The Savior promised it when He gave the sacrament to the Nephites. They were filled, and they praised Him.

We come back every week.
Windows get dusty again. That is not a failure. It is how life works. The Lord knows that. He gave us a weekly way to return, because He knew we would need it.
And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
Elder Robert D. Hales of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Out of Darkness into His Marvelous Light” from the April 2002 general conference.

When the spiritual light of the Holy Ghost is present, the darkness of Satan departs. . . . If we let the light of the Spirit flicker or fade by failing to keep the commandments or by not partaking of the sacrament or praying or studying the scriptures, the darkness of the adversary will surely come in.
Every week, one more chance to let the light in.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time about the sacrament. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: The Savior feeds the multitude

blocks.text: A crowd of thousands had followed Jesus. They were hungry, and there was little food. Jesus took five loaves and two fish, gave thanks, and fed everyone. Afterward, the next day, He told the people that He is the Bread of Life.

And Jesus took the loaves; and when he had given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to them that were set down; and likewise of the fishes as much as they would. When they were filled, he said unto his disciples, Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost. Therefore they gathered them together, and filled twelve baskets with the fragments of the five barley loaves, which remained over and above unto them that had eaten.
There was more at the end than there was at the beginning. That is what the Savior does with a small offering. A small piece of bread, given by Him, fills a hungry soul and leaves some to spare.

application.text: First, this Sunday, spend one minute before the sacrament thinking about what you want to leave behind. Be honest with yourself. Second, if something heavy is on your heart, talk to your bishop. He holds keys of mercy. Third, thank someone who helps prepare, bless, or pass the sacrament. Their service is a gift to all.

closingVerse.text: Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.

opening.text: A piano can sound beautiful in a hall. But after a few months, it drifts out of tune. No one broke it. Strings stretch. Wood shifts. The notes still sound, but something is off. A tuner comes, and with a few small turns, the whole instrument comes back into harmony.
I think of the sacrament that way. We do not stop being good people between Sundays. But we drift. A little off here. A little off there. And each week, the Lord invites us to be tuned again.
I would like to talk about what happens at the sacrament, and why it matters.

mainMessage.text: The sacrament is the ordinance Jesus gave to help us remember Him. Each week, we eat bread and drink water in memory of His body and blood. We renew our covenants. He cleanses us and promises His Spirit. It asks us to examine ourselves, with honesty and hope. And it can bring us back, a little closer to Him, every single week.

blocks.text: The first note is remembrance.

The Lord could have asked us to do many things. He asked us to remember Him. At the Last Supper, He told His apostles to do it in remembrance of Him. In the Americas, He gave the same words to the Nephites.

And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me. Likewise also the cup after supper, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you.

And this shall ye do in remembrance of my body, which I have shown unto you. And it shall be a testimony unto the Father that ye do always remember me. And if ye do always remember me ye shall have my Spirit to be with you.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles wrote about this in his article “To Always Remember Him” in the April 2011 Ensign.

We should first put in place the things that make it possible to always remember Him—frequent prayer and scripture study, thoughtful study of apostolic teachings, weekly preparation to partake of the sacrament worthily, Sunday worship, and recording and remembering what the Spirit and experience teach us about discipleship.
The sacrament is the key note. Everything else in the list is tuned to it.
The second note is promise.

Every sacrament prayer has the same shape. We ask God to bless the bread and water. We say we will take on His name, always remember Him, and keep His commandments. And He promises that we may always have His Spirit with us.

O God, the Eternal Father, we ask thee in the name of thy Son, Jesus Christ, to bless and sanctify this bread to the souls of all those who partake of it; that they may eat in remembrance of the body of thy Son, and witness unto thee, O God, the Eternal Father, that they are willing to take upon them the name of thy Son, and always remember him, and keep his commandments which he hath given them, that they may always have his Spirit to be with them. Amen.

O God, the Eternal Father, we ask thee, in the name of thy Son, Jesus Christ, to bless and sanctify this wine to the souls of all those who drink of it, that they may do it in remembrance of the blood of thy Son, which was shed for them; that they may witness unto thee, O God, the Eternal Father, that they do always remember him, that they may have his Spirit to be with them. Amen.

And it came to pass that he said unto them: Behold, here are the waters of Mormon (for thus were they called) and now, as ye are desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people, and are willing to bear one another’s burdens, that they may be light; Yea, and are willing to mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort, and to stand as witnesses of God at all times and in all things, and in all places that ye may be in, even until death, that ye may be redeemed of God, and be numbered with those of the first resurrection, that ye may have eternal life— Now I say unto you, if this be the desire of your hearts, what have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord, as a witness before him that ye have entered into a covenant with him, that ye will serve him and keep his commandments, that he may pour out his Spirit more abundantly upon you?
President Ezra Taft Benson spoke of how disciples live in his talk “Born of God” from the October 1985 general conference.
Almost every week they partake of the sacrament and witness anew to their Eternal Father that they are willing to take upon them the name of His Son, always remember Him, and keep His commandments.
The covenant we made at baptism is the pitch we are tuning to.
The third note is mercy.
When the piano is out of tune, no one is punished. It is simply fixed. The Savior did not give us the sacrament to scold us. He gave it to forgive us. His blood was shed for the remission of sins.

And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body. And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it; For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.

Thou shalt offer a sacrifice unto the Lord thy God in righteousness, even that of a broken heart and a contrite spirit. And that thou mayest more fully keep thyself unspotted from the world, thou shalt go to the house of prayer and offer up thy sacraments upon my holy day;
President Dallin H. Oaks, First Counselor in the First Presidency, taught this in his talk “The Aaronic Priesthood and the Sacrament” from the October 2019 general conference.

We are commanded to repent of our sins and to come to the Lord with a broken heart and a contrite spirit and partake of the sacrament in compliance with its covenants. When we renew our baptismal covenants in this way, the Lord renews the cleansing effect of our baptism.
We bring a broken heart. He brings the renewal.
The fourth note is the Spirit.
When a piano is in tune, it fills a room. When we are in tune with the Lord, His Spirit fills us. That is the promise He gave to the Nephites.

And he said unto them: He that eateth this bread eateth of my body to his soul; and he that drinketh of this wine drinketh of my blood to his soul; and his soul shall never hunger nor thirst, but shall be filled. Now, when the multitude had all eaten and drunk, behold, they were filled with the Spirit; and they did cry out with one voice, and gave glory to Jesus, whom they both saw and heard.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Always Have His Spirit” from the October 1996 general conference.

Let us qualify ourselves for our Savior’s promise that by partaking of the sacrament we will ‘be filled’ (3 Ne. 20:8; see also 3 Ne. 18:9), which means that we will be ‘filled with the Spirit’ (3 Ne. 20:9). That Spirit—the Holy Ghost—is our comforter, our direction finder, our communicator, our interpreter, our witness, and our purifier—our infallible guide and sanctifier for our mortal journey toward eternal life.
A comforter and a guide. He gives both to those who ask.
The tuner asks us to be honest.
A tuner listens first. He plays a note and hears what is wrong. In the same way, Paul says to examine ourselves. It is not to punish us. It is to hear what is off, so it can be put right.

Wherefore whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup. For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body.

Elder Jay E. Jensen of the Seventy shared this in his talk “Arms of Safety” from the October 2008 general conference. He was a bishop at the time, helping a young man repent. Later he watched as that young man partook again.

As I sat on the stand in that sacrament meeting, my eyes were drawn to him as he now partook of the sacrament worthily. I witnessed arms of mercy, love, and safety encircling him as the healing of the Atonement warmed his soul and lifted his load, resulting in the promised forgiveness, peace, and happiness.
Honesty is where the tuning begins. And the result is peace.
We are tuned again each week.
No one expects a piano to stay in tune forever. We should not expect to, either. That is why the sacrament comes every week, not once a year. And that is why the Lord calls Himself the bread of life.
And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
Elder Robert D. Hales of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gave this counsel in his talk “Out of Darkness into His Marvelous Light” from the April 2002 general conference.

When the spiritual light of the Holy Ghost is present, the darkness of Satan departs. . . . If we let the light of the Spirit flicker or fade by failing to keep the commandments or by not partaking of the sacrament or praying or studying the scriptures, the darkness of the adversary will surely come in.
The sacrament keeps us in tune and in the light.

story.title: The bread broken at Emmaus

blocks.text: Two disciples were walking home after the Crucifixion. They were sad and confused. A stranger joined them and talked with them about the scriptures. They invited Him to stay for supper. At the table, something happened.
And it came to pass, as he sat at meat with them, he took bread, and blessed it, and brake, and gave to them. And their eyes were opened, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight.
They knew Him in the breaking of the bread. Often we find the Lord when we are sitting still, with a simple piece of bread in our hands. That is the sacrament. It is where our eyes can be opened.

application.text: First, during the sacrament this Sunday, listen for the line in the prayer that stands out most to you. Think about it all week. Second, tell a friend or family member about a time the sacrament helped you feel the Spirit. Third, if you have been away, plan to return. The bread and water are waiting, and there is a seat for you.

opening.text: Look at a wedding ring. It is small and plain. It does not do anything. It does not light up or make a sound. But when a person looks at it, they remember. They remember a promise, and the person they made it to.
The sacrament works in a similar way. A piece of bread. A cup of water. They are simple. But when we take them, we remember a covenant, and the One who made it possible.
I would like to talk about the sacrament, and why the Savior gave it to us.

mainMessage.text: The sacrament is a weekly reminder of the Savior’s sacrifice. When we eat the bread and drink the water, we promise to take His name upon us, to remember Him, and to keep His commandments. In return, He promises His Spirit. He forgives us. He strengthens us. We come with honest hearts, and we leave with renewed hope. It is a small act that carries the greatest meaning.

blocks.text: The ring reminds us of a promise, and the sacrament reminds us of Him.
On the night before His death, Jesus broke bread and passed a cup. He told His apostles to do this in remembrance of Him. The Savior repeated the same words to the Nephites after He rose.

And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me. Likewise also the cup after supper, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you.

And this shall ye do in remembrance of my body, which I have shown unto you. And it shall be a testimony unto the Father that ye do always remember me. And if ye do always remember me ye shall have my Spirit to be with you.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his article “To Always Remember Him” in the April 2011 Ensign.

A person who wears a ring does not forget the promise. A person who takes the sacrament with care does not forget the Savior.
We say the words of the promise.
A wedding includes words. So does the sacrament. The prayers were given by the Lord and we say them the same way every week. We are asked to listen, and to say yes in our hearts.

O God, the Eternal Father, we ask thee in the name of thy Son, Jesus Christ, to bless and sanctify this bread to the souls of all those who partake of it; that they may eat in remembrance of the body of thy Son, and witness unto thee, O God, the Eternal Father, that they are willing to take upon them the name of thy Son, and always remember him, and keep his commandments which he hath given them, that they may always have his Spirit to be with them. Amen.

O God, the Eternal Father, we ask thee, in the name of thy Son, Jesus Christ, to bless and sanctify this wine to the souls of all those who drink of it, that they may do it in remembrance of the blood of thy Son, which was shed for them; that they may witness unto thee, O God, the Eternal Father, that they do always remember him, that they may have his Spirit to be with them. Amen.

And it came to pass that he said unto them: Behold, here are the waters of Mormon (for thus were they called) and now, as ye are desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people, and are willing to bear one another’s burdens, that they may be light; Yea, and are willing to mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort, and to stand as witnesses of God at all times and in all things, and in all places that ye may be in, even until death, that ye may be redeemed of God, and be numbered with those of the first resurrection, that ye may have eternal life— Now I say unto you, if this be the desire of your hearts, what have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord, as a witness before him that ye have entered into a covenant with him, that ye will serve him and keep his commandments, that he may pour out his Spirit more abundantly upon you?
President Ezra Taft Benson said this in his talk “Born of God” from the October 1985 general conference.
Almost every week they partake of the sacrament and witness anew to their Eternal Father that they are willing to take upon them the name of His Son, always remember Him, and keep His commandments.
A couple who love each other say it often, and mean it every time. The sacrament lets us do the same with the Lord.
The promise is met with forgiveness.
A covenant has two sides. We give our word. The Lord gives His. In the sacrament, He gives us cleansing. He renews what baptism began.

And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body. And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it; For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.

Thou shalt offer a sacrifice unto the Lord thy God in righteousness, even that of a broken heart and a contrite spirit. And that thou mayest more fully keep thyself unspotted from the world, thou shalt go to the house of prayer and offer up thy sacraments upon my holy day;
President Dallin H. Oaks, First Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “The Aaronic Priesthood and the Sacrament” from the October 2019 general conference.

When we fall short, we do not need to hide. We can come back and be renewed.
His Spirit is the reward of the covenant.
The Lord does not only ask. He gives. The great gift of the sacrament is the Spirit, to be with us through the week. The Nephites felt it the moment they partook.

And he said unto them: He that eateth this bread eateth of my body to his soul; and he that drinketh of this wine drinketh of my blood to his soul; and his soul shall never hunger nor thirst, but shall be filled. Now, when the multitude had all eaten and drunk, behold, they were filled with the Spirit; and they did cry out with one voice, and gave glory to Jesus, whom they both saw and heard.

That Spirit—the Holy Ghost—is our comforter, our direction finder, our communicator, our interpreter, our witness, and our purifier—our infallible guide and sanctifier for our mortal journey toward eternal life.
He gave us a promise with more in it than we can see at first.
We come with honest hearts.

The ring only means something if the promise is kept. In the same way, the sacrament asks us to be honest about where we stand. Paul says to examine ourselves. That is not to scare us. It is to help us make things right, so the sacrament can bless us.

Wherefore whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup. For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body.

Elder Jay E. Jensen of the Seventy shared this in his talk “Arms of Safety” from the October 2008 general conference. He had been the bishop of a young man who needed to repent. After a time, that young man could partake of the sacrament again.

As I sat on the stand in that sacrament meeting, my eyes were drawn to him as he now partook of the sacrament worthily. I witnessed arms of mercy, love, and safety encircling him as the healing of the Atonement warmed his soul and lifted his load, resulting in the promised forgiveness, peace, and happiness.
There is always a way back. The Lord is ready to meet us there.
A promise is renewed again and again.
Good marriages are not made on one day. They are built in small acts, repeated every week and every day. Our walk with the Savior is the same. Each week we come back to the table.
And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
Elder Robert D. Hales of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Out of Darkness into His Marvelous Light” from the April 2002 general conference.

When the spiritual light of the Holy Ghost is present, the darkness of Satan departs. . . . If we let the light of the Spirit flicker or fade by failing to keep the commandments or by not partaking of the sacrament or praying or studying the scriptures, the darkness of the adversary will surely come in.
We keep the light on by coming back, and by staying close to the One who gives it.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time about the sacrament. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: The Passover and the blood on the door

blocks.text: Before the Israelites left Egypt, the Lord gave them a sign. A lamb was killed. Its blood was placed on the door. When the destroyer passed through the land, he would see the blood and pass over that house. The Passover meal is what Jesus was eating with the apostles when He gave them the sacrament.

And the blood shall be to you for a token upon the houses where ye are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be upon you to destroy you, when I smite the land of Egypt.
The lamb stood for the Savior. The blood on the door was a sign of trust. Today the bread and water do the same. They remind us that we are protected by His sacrifice, and that we belong to Him.

Listen to every word. Third, share with a family member why the sacrament matters to you. Keep it short and sincere.
